activities.anchor: That sounds like an invasion until you learn
activities.caption: true or false — the hidden majority, audited
activities.name: mwCensusJudge

statements.s: Most microorganisms are harmful to humans.
statements.why: The overwhelming majority are harmless, and many are indispensable — digestion and much of immunity are run by resident microbes.

statements.s: The nitrogen that feeds every crop is fixed by soil bacteria.
statements.why: Alongside fermenting bread, cheese, beer and wine — and driving every nutrient cycle that keeps the visible biosphere running.

statements.s: The word "germ" refers to all microorganisms.
statements.why: It refers only to the small minority that cause disease; a microbiologist's first question is "what is it, and what is it doing?"

statements.s: Microbes in Earth's early oceans remade the planet's first atmosphere.
statements.why: The hidden majority runs the visible one — including the atmosphere itself.

activities.caption: drag between the two halves of Pasteur's flask
activities.name: mwSwanCompare

config.prompt: One flask, two fates — drag between them:

before.label: neck intact
before.text: Air enters, but dust and its microbial passengers settle in the S-bend and never reach the broth — which stays sterile indefinitely.

after.label: neck broken
after.text: Dust reaches the broth and it spoils. Microbes come from other microbes — the negative result that made the germ theory of disease thinkable.

config.why: It took a cleverly controlled experiment, not a cleverer person, to falsify spontaneous generation: science replaced plausible inference with controlled comparison.

activities.anchor: prized merely for reaching the limit
activities.caption: one line of the optics note oversells the oil
activities.name: mwLimitSpot

config.prompt: An optics note — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: Most bacteria are 1–5 micrometres across — a micrometre is a millionth of a metre.
A light microscope cannot distinguish two points closer than about 0.2 µm, roughly half the wavelength of visible light.
The limit is physics, not engineering: no grinding of lenses can beat it.
Oil-immersion objectives replace air with oil that matches the glass, reaching cleanly past the light limit to 0.02 µm.
Going beyond 0.2 µm required a completely different kind of instrument — the electron microscope.
config.correction: Oil-immersion objectives are prized merely for reaching the 0.2 µm limit cleanly — they do not beat it. Beating the wavelength of light took the electron microscope, at the price of never imaging a living specimen.
config.why: The floor is diffraction: roughly half the wavelength of visible light, set by physics.

activities.anchor: still usually the first test run on an unknown bacterium
activities.caption: file each genus by its Gram reaction
activities.name: mwGramBuckets

config.prompt: The stain's colour is a report on wall architecture — file each genus:
buckets: Gram-negative — thin layer plus outer membrane, takes pink
config.why: The colour predicts antibiotic susceptibility: many antibiotics target peptidoglycan synthesis, so penicillin works better against Gram-positives — the first fork in every identification key.

activities.anchor: it narrows thousands of species to a family of suspects
activities.caption: bet what the stain actually reports
activities.name: mwStainPredict

config.q: A laboratory reports "Gram-negative rods" from a culture. What has the stain told you?
choices: One architectural fact that sorts the unknown into one of two enormous classes.
Which antibiotic will treat the infection.
config.why: A stain is a chapter heading, not the book: the species itself still needs culture, biochemical tests or sequencing to name.

activities.anchor: a key built on appearance can put unrelated organisms together
activities.caption: pair each domain — and the molecule that found them
activities.name: mwDomainsMatch

config.prompt: The three-domain system — pair each entry with its description:

pairs.right: the prokaryotes of everyday laboratory work — E. coli and cousins
prokaryotes with eukaryote-like information machinery, often in extremes — and, so far, no human diseases identified
everything with a nucleus — protists, fungi, plants, animals
present in every cell, essential, slowly evolving — so it records deep ancestry

config.why: Woese found a gulf nobody had suspected: the "bacteria" split into two groups as different from each other as either is from us — and Bergey's Manual reorganised itself around the phylogenetic principle.

activities.caption: walk the naming unit an outbreak report needs
activities.name: mwStrainBranch

config.root: A headline announces an "E. coli outbreak". Which unit of the name carries the story?

start.text: What does the report need to specify to be meaningful?

choices.label: The species — Escherichia coli
choices.feedback: Far too coarse: the species contains both laboratory citizens and pathogens.

choices.label: The strain — surface antigens and toxins
The genus — Escherichia
choices.feedback: Honours an ancestry — useful for naming, too broad for tracking.

species.text: E. coli K-12 is a harmless gut laboratory citizen; E. coli O157:H7 is a dangerous pathogen. Same species, a handful of acquired genes apart — the species cannot carry the clinical story.

strain.text: Strains of one species can behave as differently as a laboratory citizen and a lethal pathogen. Diagnosis and treatment hang on the strain — its surface antigens and its toxins.

genus.text: The genus groups genuinely related organisms — Theodor Escherich lent it his name — but the epithet ("of the colon") and the strain are where the working detail sits.

config.why: The biological species concept fails for organisms that exchange genes sideways — bacterial species are pragmatic clusters, and the strain is where behaviour lives.

activities.anchor: a swab from a sore throat
activities.caption: rebuild the three-programme workup of one swab
activities.name: mwSwabOrder

config.prompt: One swab, three programmes — drag the workup into order:
items: Seeing, first and fastest: a Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains, pointing toward Streptococcus
Growing, overnight: a blood-agar plate shows small colonies with clear haloes of beta-haemolysis
A catalase test plus a bacitracin disc discriminate Streptococcus pyogenes from look-alikes
Reading, where needed: a species-specific gene read directly, bypassing culture entirely
config.why: Each step was invented by the people on the timeline — and a modern diagnostic laboratory runs the history of microbiology at production speed.
